Self-Rewarded Reinforcement Learning for Better-Structured Medical Explanations in Small Language Models

Prakhar Mishra Email: 443prakharmishra@gmail.com Affiliation: Department of Information Technology, Delhi Technological University, New Delhi, India    Bhavya Yajush Awasthi Email: bhavya.yajush@gmail.com Affiliation: Indian Institute of Technology, Guwahati, Guwahati, Assam, India Affiliation: Delhi Skill and Entrepreneurship University, New Delhi, India    Tanuja Email: shalus384@gmail.com Affiliation: Central University of Haryana, Mahendragarh, Haryana, India    Nishant Email: nishantsinghchauhan0010@gmail.com Affiliation: Department of Information Technology, Delhi Technological University, New Delhi, India
Abstract

Small language models (SLMs) can run on commodity hardware and support privacy-preserving, on-premises clinical deployment, but their medical explanations are often short and poorly structured compared with large language models. Recent supervised approaches such as Meerkat transfer chain-of-thought reasoning into 7B–8B backbones, yet their training objective does not directly target the style or organization of the generated rationales. Building on the instruction-tuned Mistral-7B backbone, we investigate whether a lightweight reinforcement learning (RL) step can improve explanation structure without human preference labels. We apply Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with LoRA adaptation to 2,000 Meerkat-derived medical prompts, guided by a simple self-supervised reward that favors longer, lexically diverse, and well-punctuated responses while penalizing very short ones. Training for about 170 PPO steps on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU yields a stable increase in the average reward. Quantitative and qualitative comparisons show that the RL-tuned model produces longer, more organized, multi-point explanations while preserving the underlying medical content. We discuss the promise and the limitations of self-rewarded RL for shaping the style of medical explanations.

keywords
large language models, small language models, medical AI, reinforcement learning, PPO, LoRA, instruction tuning, chain-of-thought

1 Introduction

Large language models have shown great promise in question-answering in medicine, case reasoning, and decision-making in the clinical domain. However, the application of these models in the healthcare industry is limited due to privacy and computational concerns.Singhal et al. (2023); Nori et al. (2023) Closed models like GPT-4 and Med-PaLM 2 can perform at or better than the level of a human in USMLE tests, but they are not deployable in the cloud due to confidentiality and compliance concerns.Singhal et al. (2023) On the other hand, open SLMs with fewer than ten billion parameters can be run on a single high-end GPU and are deployable in the healthcare industry.Kim et al. (2025); Wu et al. (2023); Chen et al. (2023) However, SLMs have been observed to perform poorly in tasks that involve multi-step reasoning, long context synthesis, and structured explanation.Kim et al. (2025); Labrak et al. (2024)

The Meerkat series of medical SLMs have been designed to bridge this performance gap by using chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning traces from the GPT-4 model and transferring this reasoning ability into the 7B and 8B parameter backbones Mistral-7B and Llama-3-8B, respectively, in combination with synthetic QA pairs from 18 medical textbooks and several instruction following datasets.Kim et al. (2025) Fine-tuning the backbones of the SLMs on the combination of CoT and instruction following data results in SLMs that perform better than the existing 7B medical LMs and even the GPT-3.5 model on various multiple-choice exams such as MedQA and MedMCQA while remaining deployable in the on-premises environment.Kim et al. (2025); Jin et al. (2020); Pal et al. (2022) This demonstrates that carefully targeted supervision can endow SLMs with strong reasoning skills without resorting to extremely large parameter counts.

In particular, reinforcement learning techniques such as Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)Schulman et al. (2017) have come to dominate the field of alignment for LLMs with human preferences, as encapsulated by various instances of the reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) family of approaches used for InstructGPT and similar models.Ouyang et al. (2022); Ziegler et al. (2019) While most existing approaches in this space have focused on large models or used expensive human/model-based preference labels for pairs of outputs, it remains an open question for small medical language models: can a lightweight RL step, using a simple self-supervised proxy reward, be used to improve the structure of the generated explanations beyond what supervised CoT training can achieve.

This paper seeks to answer that question with an in-depth experimental design. Beginning with the openly available Mistral-7B-Instruct backbone,Jiang et al. (2023) we utilize PPOSchulman et al. (2017) with LoRA adaptationHu et al. (2021) using the TRL libraryHugging Face (2023) on a subset of Meerkat’s CoT-style medical instruction data.Kim et al. (2025) The reward function is kept simple: it rewards longer outputs within a certain length, lexical diversity, and a bonus if there is punctuation at the end of sentences, while penalizing very short outputs. While such a reward does not reflect clinical accuracy, it does directly affect explanation length and structure, which is an important dimension in the limitations and future work sections of Meerkat and similar medical LMs.Kim et al. (2025); Wu et al. (2023); Chen et al. (2023)

We summarize our contributions as follows:

  1. 1.

    We propose a lightweight reinforcement learning pipeline for improving explanation structure in medical small language models using PPO with LoRA adaptation.

  2. 2.

    We design a fully automatic proxy reward function based on response length, lexical diversity, and sentence boundary signals, enabling reinforcement learning alignment without human preference labels.

  3. 3.

    Through both quantitative and qualitative analysis, we demonstrate that reinforcement learning can improve the structural organization of medical explanations generated by small language models.

  4. 4.

    Our results highlight that reinforcement learning can be used not only to align language models with human preferences but also to control structural properties of generated explanations.

2 Background and related work

2.1 Medical small language models

There is an increasing amount of work on domain-specialized language models in medicine and healthcare. Previous work has focused on fine-tuning general-purpose LLMs using continuous pre-training on biomedical data such as PubMed and clinical notes. This has led to the creation of models like PMC-LLaMA, Me-LLaMA, and other variants of LLaMA specialized in medicine.Wu et al. (2023); Xie et al. (2024) While these models improve the knowledge base of medical information, improvements in multi-step reasoning capabilities are less impressive in proportion to the pre-training cost.

Meerkat proposes an alternate approach that does not rely on expensive pre-training. Instead, it focuses on curating high-quality CoT datasets by prompting GPT-4 on MedQA datasets and medical textbooks. Fine-tuning 7B and 8B backbones on the combined CoT and instruction-following datasets results in models that outperform previous 7B medical LMs like MediTron-7B, BioMistral-7B, and GPT-3.5 on multiple-choice exams.Kim et al. (2025); Chen et al. (2023); Labrak et al. (2024) This approach shows that supervision over reasoning traces can narrow the performance gap between medical LMs and even very large, expensive models like Med-PaLM and Med-PaLM 2.Singhal et al. (2023)

Other medical LMs also investigate domain-specific adaptation: ChatDoctor, MedInstruct-52K, and other instruction-tuned models focusing on patient–doctor dialogue and consumer health-related queries.Li et al. (2023); Zhang et al. (2023) These studies emphasize the need to consider the alignment of the output with the context of medical communication beyond the results of the exam.

2.2 Medical QA benchmarks

Multiple-choice medical question answer benchmarks like MedQA and MedMCQA have become the standard in assessing the knowledge and reasoning abilities of LLMs in the medical domain.Jin et al. (2020); Pal et al. (2022) MedQA is based on USMLE questions in various languages from professional board exams, while MedMCQA is based on almost 200k questions in 21 subjects from Indian entrance exams.Jin et al. (2020); Pal et al. (2022) These two are the basis for the evaluation protocols of Meerkat, Med-PaLM, PMC-LLaMA, MEDITRON, and BioMistral.Kim et al. (2025); Singhal et al. (2023); Wu et al. (2023); Chen et al. (2023); Labrak et al. (2024)

Apart from the exam-oriented QA, the MultiMedQA system aggregates six existing medical QA datasets with the HealthSearchQA dataset of consumer health queries and presents a framework for human evaluation based on criteria like factuality, precision, potential harm, and bias.Singhal et al. (2023) This broader outlook again points out that success in multiple-choice tests does not imply safe practice in the real world.

2.3 Reinforcement learning for language models

However, reinforcement learning has emerged as one of the main approaches to align LLMs with human preferences and downstream objectives. Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) is one of the most popular on-policy policy gradient methods, in which a clipped version of the surrogate objective is maximized in order to ensure that the policy change remains in a ‘trust region’ around the old policy.Schulman et al. (2017) For LLMs, PPO is usually used in conjunction with a reference model and a value function head, in which a reward is optimized that consists of a scalar quality signal (such as a human preference score) as well as a KL term that encourages the fine-tuned model to stay close to the reference model.Ziegler et al. (2019); Ouyang et al. (2022)

The RLHF paradigm that is instantiated by InstructGPT and subsequent models uses PPO in addition to supervised fine-tuning, with a supervised reward learning component that is trained on human preference data.Ziegler et al. (2019); Ouyang et al. (2022) More recent work has focused on newer RL regimes that prioritize step-by-step reasoning performance.Wei et al. (2022); Zhu et al. (2023) However, existing studies focus on larger general-purpose models.

A good implementation of PPO for transformer-based language models can be found in the TRL library, including AutoModelForCausalLMWithValueHead and PPOTrainer classes.Hugging Face (2023) Together with parameter-efficient adaptation approaches like LoRA, this makes it feasible for researchers to test RL alignment approaches using their home computers.

2.4 Parameter-efficient adaptation

“Low-Rank Adaptation” (LoRA) is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that keeps the original weights of the model fixed and adds small matrices to be learned to the linear layers that the model will be fine-tuned on.Hu et al. (2021) Instead of learning the entire weight matrix WW for the linear layers, the weights Δ​W\Delta W will be learned in a low-rank factorized form B​ABA where AA and BB have much lower ranks than the original weights. This will result in a much lower number of parameters to be learned for the model.

LoRA is part of a larger group of methods that are referred to as “adapter-based.” The idea behind these methods is that the backbone of the network is frozen, and the adapters are small modules that are added for the specific task at hand.Houlsby et al. (2019); Pfeiffer et al. (2020) More recently, there has been the introduction of QLoRA, where the idea is that the combination of 4-bit quantization and the use of adapters for the task at hand allows for the fine-tuning of large models (65B parameters) on a single GPU without sacrificing performance.Dettmers et al. (2023) The combination of PPO and LoRA for the task of RL for LLMs allows the policy and value functions to be updated using only a small fraction of the total number of parameters, which is particularly appealing for the case of 7B-scale models running on a single GPU.

3 Method

3.1 Problem setting

We assume an instruction-following single-turn medical context in which the model is given a prompt in natural language xx that corresponds to a medical query, symptom description, or conceptual query and is asked to produce an answer yy that provides an explanation of relevant concepts and information, possible reasons and explanations, and recommendations and actions to take. Mathematically speaking, the language model is viewed as a policy πθ​(y∣x)\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x) over sequences of tokens, and the aim is to adjust the parameters θ\theta so that the produced explanation meets certain criteria in terms of length, diversity, and sentence structure while retaining the learned medical content from the instruction tuning.

Here, f⁡(y)f(y) is defined as the textual reward associated with the generated answer based on surface-level statistics, as described below. Our objective is to maximize the expected reward under the policy,

J(θ)=𝔼x∼D,y∼πθ(⋅∣x)[f(y)],J(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim D,\,y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)}[f(y)], (1)

where DD is a fixed dataset of medical prompts derived from Meerkat’s instruction corpus.Kim et al. (2025)

3.2 Base model and dataset

We load it from the mistralai/Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 checkpoint, a 7B parameter decoder-only transformer with grouped query attention and instruction tuning pretraining for general-purpose dialogue.Jiang et al. (2023) This is used both as the reference and initial policy. It has been pre-trained on web-scale data but has not been fine-tuned with the specialized CoT supervision used in Meerkat or other medical SLMs like PMC-LLaMA, MEDITRON, or BioMistral.Kim et al. (2025); Wu et al. (2023); Chen et al. (2023); Labrak et al. (2024)

To add medical domain knowledge and structure to the reasoning, we fine-tune on the JSONL dataset meerkat_rl_subset.jsonl containing 2,000 prompts that were randomly selected from the instruction tuning data released by Meerkat.Kim et al. (2025) This is a self-contained medical query or instruction that is usually in the form of medical questions, USMLE questions, synthetic questions generated from textbooks, or patient-doctor conversations. The variety of the sampled prompts includes different types of medical instructions such as patient inquiries based on symptoms, explanations based on concepts for physiological processes, medical examination questions, and health advice scenarios. This diversity exposes the model to both diagnostic reasoning and explanatory tasks during reinforcement learning. For our initial experiment, we use PPO only on the prompts and do not condition on the original Meerkat rationales, delegating explanation generation entirely to the policy.

The tokenizer used for tokenizing the prompt is Mistral. It has a maximum input length of 256 tokens and left padding. It generates up to 200 new tokens per rollout in PPO training and evaluation.

3.3 Reward design

The reward function f⁡(y)f(y) is a deterministic function that takes the generated answer text yy and returns a scalar value in approximately the range [0.01,1.3][0.01,1.3]. The reward function can be defined as a sum of four terms:

  1. 1.

    Length reward. Let nn be the number of whitespace-separated tokens in yy. We define

    flen​(y)=min⁡(n50, 1),f_{\text{len}}(y)=\min\left(\frac{n}{50},\,1\right), (2)

    which increases linearly with length up to 50 tokens and saturates thereafter.

  2. 2.

    Diversity reward. Let V⁡(y)V(y) be the set of unique tokens in yy. We define the lexical diversity term as

    fdiv​(y)=|V⁡(y)|n+10−6,f_{\text{div}}(y)=\frac{|V(y)|}{n+10^{-6}}, (3)

    encouraging a higher ratio of unique words to total words.

  3. 3.

    Punctuation bonus. To encourage explicit sentence boundaries, we add a fixed bonus if the text contains at least one sentence-ending punctuation mark:

    fpunc​(y)={0.3,if y contains any of .,!?,0,otherwise.f_{\text{punc}}(y)=\begin{cases}0.3,&\text{if }y\text{ contains any of }.,!?,\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (4)
  4. 4.

    Short-output penalty. Extremely short responses are penalized via

    fshort​(y)={−0.3,n<5,0,otherwise.f_{\text{short}}(y)=\begin{cases}-0.3,&n<5,\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (5)

The total reward is the sum

f⁡(y)=flen​(y)+fdiv​(y)+fpunc​(y)+fshort​(y),f(y)=f_{\text{len}}(y)+f_{\text{div}}(y)+f_{\text{punc}}(y)+f_{\text{short}}(y), (6)

clamped from below at 0.010.01 to avoid zero rewards. This proxy explicitly encourages longer, lexically rich, and sentence-structured outputs while disfavoring trivial or single-word responses. Notably, it does not encode any notion of medical correctness or safety, so the policy must rely on prior supervised training for factuality.Ziegler et al. (2019); Ouyang et al. (2022)

3.4 PPO fine-tuning with LoRA

We perform the RL fine-tuning using PPO and the TRL library.Hugging Face (2023) Both the policy and the value function share the same backbone, which is based on the Transformer architecture and implemented using AutoModelForCausalLMWithValueHead. On top of this backbone, we use a LoRA configuration that will be applied on the query, key, value, and output projection matrices (q_proj, k_proj, v_proj, o_proj). We use a rank r=16r=16, a scaling factor α=32\alpha=32, and a dropout probability of 0.050.05.Hu et al. (2021) All original Mistral weights are frozen; only the LoRA adapters and value head parameters are trainable.

The PPO is set with a batch size of 4 prompts per update, a minibatch size of 2, learning rate 10−610^{-6}, initial KL coefficient 0.5, and target KL divergence 3.0. The rollouts are generated by the current policy using nucleus sampling (topp=0.9\text{top}_{p}=0.9), temperature 0.7, repetition penalty 1.1, and maximum 200 new tokens. The KL penalty is computed against a frozen reference model, initialized from the same checkpoint before RL training.Ziegler et al. (2019); Ouyang et al. (2022)

The clipped PPO surrogate objective for a batch of trajectories can be written as

LPPO(θ)=𝔼t[min(rt​(θ)​A^t,clip(rt(θ),1−ϵ,1+ϵ)A^t)],\begin{split}L^{\text{PPO}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{t}\bigl[\min\bigl(&r_{t}(\theta)\,\hat{A}_{t},\;\\ &\operatorname{clip}(r_{t}(\theta),1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)\,\hat{A}_{t}\bigr)\bigr],\end{split} (7)

where rt​(θ)r_{t}(\theta) is the ratio of the policy probability at the given token position tt for the new and old policies, A^t\hat{A}_{t} is the advantage estimate, and ϵ\epsilon is the clipping parameter.Schulman et al. (2017) In our case, the advantages are calculated for each token by the generalized advantage estimation and are summed over the sequence.Hugging Face (2023)

Training is run for 170–180 PPO steps, periodically saving checkpoints every 10 steps. All experiments are conducted on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU in a Google Colab environment and all experiments were conducted using the Hugging Face Transformers and TRL libraries with deterministic random seeds to ensure reproducibility of training runs.

4 Experiments

4.1 Training dynamics

In the plot shown in Figure 1, the average scalar reward over each PPO update cycle is tracked over 160+ updates. At the beginning of the training process, the average reward is seen to vary between the minimum clamp value of 0.01 and approximately 0.5. As training progresses, more updates with high average reward are seen, with long sequences of updates yielding average rewards between 0.45 and 0.55, with occasional spikes in reward up to 1.0 for long, diverse, well-punctuated outputs.

The role of individual components in the proxy reward function is also explored to better understand the evolution of the model’s behavior during training. In particular, the evolution of the reward for increasing lengths, lexical diversity, and punctuation bonus within PPO updates is studied to better understand the behavior of the reward signal in improving the structure of the explanations. As illustrated in Figure 2, the model is seen to be optimizing for longer and better-structured outputs over time.

The important hyperparameters and data-related information are provided in Table 1. As seen, the PPO objective is always optimized with respect to the proxy reward, even with a limited batch size and data, showing that, indeed, the model is adapting its surface-level generation behavior, especially in the increase in response length over time, as depicted in Figure 3.

The total reinforcement learning training process took about 2–3 hours using a single NVIDIA A100 GPU with the Google Colab environment. The number of trainable parameters remains approximately 13.6M since we are only updating the LoRA adapters and the value head parameters. This is a relatively small number compared to the full 7B backbone parameters, which shows that reinforcement learning style alignment can be achieved with relatively low computational resources for medical SLMs.

4.2 Quantitative analysis of explanation structure

While the qualitative analysis suggests that the RL-tuned model produces more structured explanations, we perform a simple quantitative analysis of the explanations produced.

We calculate three surface-level metrics on a held-out set of 100 prompts: average length of the response in tokens, lexical diversity (measured as Distinct-1), and average number of sentences in a response.

Table 2 summarizes the comparison between the base model and the RL-tuned model.

The RL-tuned model consistently produces longer and more structurally segmented responses, which aligns with the intended optimization behavior of the proxy reward function.

4.3 Qualitative evaluation on clinical prompts

To assess the impact of RL fine-tuning on explanation style, we qualitatively compare the base and RL-tuned models on a set of five representative prompts:

  1. 1.

    “I have had a headache for 3 days and it is getting worse. What should I do?”

  2. 2.

    “What is insulin and why do people with diabetes need it?”

  3. 3.

    “What causes a fever and when should someone worry about it?”

  4. 4.

    “I feel chest pain after exercise. Is this serious?”

  5. 5.

    “What are early warning signs of a stroke?”

For each prompt, we sample one text from the base model Mistral-7B-Instruct and one text from the RL-tuned checkpoint at step 150, using the same decoding parameters. Table 3 summarizes the main stylistic differences.

To complement the table, Figure 10 sketches the qualitative evaluation pipeline, from prompt selection through generation and manual comparison. This schematic can be instantiated later with actual diagrams based on saved generations.

On the whole, the RL-tuned model is seen to provide longer, more structured, and more explicitly enumerated explanations compared to the base model. The answer is composed of multiple sentences in paragraphs or implicit bullet points that cover definitions, reasons, home management, and escalation criteria. The answer is in line with the reward signal that favors longer responses with diversity and punctuation in sentences.

In an attempt to create an even more transparent view of these differences, Figures 5–9 offer prompt-wise visualizations in an overlapping manner by using the original response generated by both models. It is worth mentioning that these figures are provided without any paraphrasing in an attempt to allow the reader to examine the difference created by the application of reinforcement learning in terms of the structure, level of detail, etc. With respect to the overall structure of the response, it is clear that the RL-tuned model is more robust in terms of organization, sequencing, etc.

Collectively, these examples illustrate that, in its responses, the RL-tuned model is not only producing longer text, but also text that is more structured around relevant medical guidance. The qualitative improvements can be seen particularly in those prompts for which the answer is aided by a checklist-style structure, escalation guidance, or a division of general explanation and next steps. Of course, these findings are based only on a small prompt set, but they do support the general hypothesis that reinforcement learning with a simple proxy reward could improve the presentation style of medical explanations, even when the factual content is similar across approaches.

Most notably, the RL-tuned model is not seen to have any apparent degradation in factuality under these small-scale qualitative tests. The additional information is more an expansion of the information that the base model is already implicitly providing. However, without further evaluation and testing with benchmarks and experts, no claims about safety and reliability are made.Singhal et al. (2023)

4.4 Ablation and sensitivity considerations

Though full ablation studies will be left for future work, there are a few design choices that we think it is useful to discuss:

  1. 1.

    Reward scaling. The reward function has several terms of similar magnitude, but the constant reward of 0.3 punctuation bonus and −0.3-0.3 short output penalty dominate when answers are very short. This is probably why we see many instances of the minimum clamped reward of 0.01 in our reward curves when the policy is producing short answers.

  2. 2.

    Batch size and exploration. The PPO batch size of only four prompts per step means that there is a lot of variance in our advantage estimation. Increasing our batch size or using more aggressive entropy regularization could improve our training dynamics.Schulman et al. (2017)

  3. 3.

    Checkpoint selection. The differences in our checkpoints around steps 100, 150, and 170 are fairly subtle. In practice, we select a checkpoint based on a validation metric that is a better proxy for explanation quality than reward.

Figure 4 is a high-level overview of our overall method, including model initialization, dataset preparation, PPO rollouts, reward computation, and LoRA adapter updates.

4.5 Training stability

To ensure that the observed improvements in behavior are not specific to the run, we also ran the PPO fine-tuning multiple times with different random seeds. The qualitative trends were consistent in all runs, especially the increase in response length and structural organization provided by the proxy reward function. Although there were slight variations in the reward curves because of the stochastic nature of the PPO algorithm, the overall improvement in the structure was consistent.

5 Discussion

Our findings indicate that the simple self-supervised reward signal can have an impact on the style of explanations generated by the medical SLM using PPO and parameter-efficient adaptation. The RL-trained model tends to produce multi-step enumerated answers that clearly distinguish differential diagnoses, warning signs, and action items. Although the CoT training signal emphasizes the content and logic of reasoning traces, the surface features such as the number of words and punctuation are not explicitly optimized for.Wei et al. (2022); Kim et al. (2025) These results suggest that reinforcement learning can influence not only factual accuracy but also stylistic and structural aspects of explanations generated by small language models.

The drawbacks of the approach are substantial. The reward signal is completely unaware of medical correctness and safety. The model could, in theory, receive high rewards for generating long, diverse, yet medically incorrect explanations. Although we did not observe such effects in our small-scale qualitative evaluation, the reason is probably that the instruction-tuned Mistral backbone already contains good medical priors. Yet, we cannot assume that in other cases.Singhal et al. (2023); Chen et al. (2023)

Second, there is no reward for human preferences, only a proxy reward, meaning improvements are only ensured with respect to this proxy reward, not any form of quality. The issue of reward hacking, in which the model learns degenerate ways of optimizing the reward, is still an open problem, particularly for longer training times or larger datasets.Ziegler et al. (2019); Ouyang et al. (2022)

Third, our study is limited in scale. We only use 2,000 prompts, one GPU, and short training times. For a paper in a high-impact venue, a larger study is needed, including quantitative evaluation of MedQA, MedMCQA, NEJM Case Challenges, comparison with Meerkat-7B/8B, as well as other larger general-purpose models, user studies with clinicians, as well as robustness studies across prompt distributions.Jin et al. (2020); Pal et al. (2022); Kim et al. (2025); Wu et al. (2023)

6 Limitations and future work

This work can be considered a pilot study to demonstrate the potential of applying reinforcement learning to guide CoT-style medical instruction tuning for explanation style. Several avenues for future work can be identified:

  1. 1.

    Rewards from clinically informed sources. Replacing or supplementing the proxy reward with rewards based on retrieval augmented generation, medical guidelines, or weak supervision from knowledge sources. For example, the reward could be based on the number of generated outputs that do not contradict the generated medical guidelines.Singhal et al. (2023); Wu et al. (2023)

  2. 2.

    Preference-based alignment. Utilizing human or expert preferences for pairs of medical explanations to fine-tune a reward function, similar to RLHF approaches.Ziegler et al. (2019); Ouyang et al. (2022)

  3. 3.

    Benchmark evaluation. Evaluating the RL-tuned model on existing medical QA benchmarks and comparing it to existing models such as Meerkat-7B, Meerkat-8B, PMC-LLaMA, MEDITRON, BioMistral, to identify potential trade-offs between styles and accuracy.Jin et al. (2020); Pal et al. (2022); Kim et al. (2025); Wu et al. (2023); Chen et al. (2023); Labrak et al. (2024)

  4. 4.

    Smaller backbones. Extending the same approach to even smaller backbones (e.g., 3B or lower) to investigate the extent to which reasoning-style improvements can be achieved with lower hardware budgets.

  5. 5.

    Safety and calibration. Study how RL-modified explanation style interacts with uncertainty calibration, hallucination rates, and user trust, particularly in high-stakes settings.Singhal et al. (2023)

7 Conclusion

We have outlined a reinforcement learning process that uses PPO with a minimal LoRA adaptation to fine-tune a 7B parameter instruction-tuned language model in a medical context, with a self-supervised reward function that promotes longer, more diverse, and sentence-structured explanations. Our process was successful in optimizing a proxy reward function over a subset of Meerkat’s medical instruction data, producing qualitatively better structured explanations over real-world clinical data. Although effective for influencing explanation style in small medical language models, this process is, by itself, not sufficient as a solution for deployment in a clinical context. The way to bridge this gap to a solution suitable for deployment in a clinical context is by adding in clinically motivated reward signals, human preferences, evaluation, and safety.Singhal et al. (2023); Kim et al. (2025)

Reinforcement learning objectives should be carefully designed to avoid encouraging unsafe or misleading behavior, and domain experts should be involved in both evaluation and oversight. Not applicable.

Data and code availability

The reinforcement learning experiments described in this manuscript are implemented in a Jupyter notebook based on the TRL library, using the publicly released Meerkat instruction data and the mistralai/Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 model. Kim et al. (2025); Jiang et al. (2023); Hugging Face (2023)
